If you have a wind- or waterproof jacket, wear it to keep out wind, rain and wet snow.
Wool or synthetic clothing is better than cotton. Cotton soaks up water and won't keep you warm when it's wet.
Keep your feet as dry as you can.
Stay calm and think through your situation.
If you're waiting for help, rest, save your energy and wait patiently.
If you have a whistle, blow it often. It helps people find you and saves the energy you'd use yelling.
If you have a flashlight, flash SOS: three quick flashes, three slow, then three quick.
If you have a mirror, flash it toward planes or helicopters flying nearby.
Lay out brightly colored clothing in an open clearing where searchers can see it.

turns.user: I'm on a sunny section of the Arizona Trail outside Tucson and feel wiped out. We're low on shade but still have water.
steps: Rest in the shade.
If you have a wide-brimmed hat, wear it to shield your face and neck from the sun.
Avoid hard activity during the hottest part of the day if you can.
Drink plenty of water, even if you don't feel thirsty.
The temperature inside a parked vehicle can rapidly rise to a dangerous level for children, pets and even adults.
Don't ration your drinking water unless authorities tell you to. Drink what you need today and try to find more for tomorrow.
Streams, rivers and other moving water can be sources of water.
Water from outdoor sources must be treated to kill germs before you drink it.
If the water might have fuel or chemicals in it, don't drink it. Boiling won't make it safe.
If the water is cloudy, first filter it through a clean cloth, paper towel or coffee filter.
Bring clear water to a rolling boil for 1 minute. Above 6,500 feet, boil it for 3 minutes.
Do not drink seawater. Drinking seawater can be deadly to humans.
Melt snow before drinking it. Eating unmelted snow will lower your body temperature.

steps: Stay with your vehicle and try not to panic.
Before running the engine, make sure the exhaust pipe isn't blocked.
In the cold, run the engine about 10 minutes each hour for warmth, with a window open a little to keep out carbon monoxide.
Make your car easy to see: tie brightly colored cloth to a mirror, door handle or antenna.
At night, turn on the inside light while the engine is running.
In snow and wind, if you leave your vehicle you will become disoriented quickly.
After snow stops falling, raise the hood to show you need help.
Keep children close to you.
Watch children closely and never let them run ahead of you.
If you are with others in a stranded vehicle, take turns sleeping.
In heat, children, infants and older adults should stay in the coolest available place.
Never leave a child unattended in a vehicle, even with the windows down, even for just a minute.
As soon as you have signal, call 911.
Call if you can, text if you can't. Some areas accept texts to 911, but a voice call is best.
Be ready to tell them where you are, as exactly as you can.
Tell them the phone number you're calling from.
Tell them what the emergency is.
Don't hang up until the call-taker tells you to.
Find shelter. Try to stay dry and cover all exposed skin.
If there's no shelter, build a lean-to or windbreak to block the wind.
If you have a wind- or waterproof jacket, wear it to keep out wind, rain and wet snow.
Wool or synthetic clothing is better than cotton. Cotton soaks up water and won't keep you warm when it's wet.
Keep your feet as dry as you can.

If you have a map, compass or GPS, or can see landmarks, use them to try to work out where you are.
If it's safe, retrace your steps to get back to the route you planned.
If you can't safely find your way back, stay where you are.
Changing location will make it hard for searchers to find you. Move only if there is an immediate threat to life.
Don't ration your drinking water unless authorities tell you to. Drink what you need today and try to find more for tomorrow.
Streams, rivers and other moving water can be sources of water.
Water from outdoor sources must be treated to kill germs before you drink it.
If the water might have fuel or chemicals in it, don't drink it. Boiling won't make it safe.
If the water is cloudy, first filter it through a clean cloth, paper towel or coffee filter.
Bring clear water to a rolling boil for 1 minute. Above 6,500 feet, boil it for 3 minutes.
Do not drink seawater. Drinking seawater can be deadly to humans.
Melt snow before drinking it. Eating unmelted snow will lower your body temperature.
